query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, uniform Ni interlayer coating on tungsten particles before copper infiltration will enhance interfacial wetting and bonding, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation during processing and yielding a W–Cu composite with improved thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation compared to conventional, uncoated composites.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or a connected W skeleton embedded in or mixed with a Cu matrix produced by conventional powder consolidation methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering or vapor-coated powders without an interlayer).
generation.intervention: Introduce a single processing step of depositing a thin Ni film on the surfaces of W particles via vapor deposition before copper infiltration and subsequent sintering.
generation.conditions: Processing to be performed in a high-vacuum environment with controlled temperature parameters to ensure a uniform Ni coating; service conditions include exposure to high thermal loads and irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joint environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni interlayer promotes intimate contact between W and Cu by improving wettability and interfacial adhesion, thereby minimizing voids and defects at the phase boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The Ni layer acts as a wetting agent that reduces surface energy mismatch between molten Cu and W, fostering a more uniform microstructure during sintering and limiting phase separation, which in turn improves both thermal conductivity and mechanical strength under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline composite produced without an interlayer, the Ni-coated composite is expected to exhibit fewer interfacial voids, enhanced thermal conductivity, and greater mechanical durability during thermal cycling and irradiation exposure.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites fabricated by current methods (e.g., spark-plasma sintering of vapor-coated W powders or mechanical alloying) that do not include an interlayer treatment and thus are prone to void formation and phase separation.
generation.boundary: Processing boundary: vapor deposition of Ni and sintering conditions optimized for fusion-reactor joint applications; Service boundary: performance under thermal and irradiation conditions typical of fusion environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical integrity, as well as the long-term stability of the Ni interlayer under irradiation, remain uncertain and warrant experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with a pre-sintering vapor-deposited Ni interlayer on the W particles and one set processed by an identical route without the Ni coating. Subject both sets to identical sintering conditions and then to simulated fusion-reactor service conditions including thermal cycling and irradiation.
measurements: High-resolution electron microscopy to assess interfacial integrity and void fraction
Thermal conductivity assessments (e.g., laser flash analysis)
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile strength, fracture toughness) before and after irradiation
Quantitative image analysis of phase distribution and bonding quality at the W–Cu interface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not display statistically significant improvements in interfacial bonding, reduced voiding, enhanced thermal conductivity, and greater mechanical durability compared to the uncoated baseline, or if the Ni layer degrades adversely under irradiation, then the hypothesis is falsified.
